docs.title: Winnie's Computed
docs.text:
Lua node-graph programming for NeoForge 1.21.1 — visual scripting with a sandboxed Lua runtime.

Get started View on GitHub

docs.title: About
docs.text:
Fork of The Propulsion Team's Computed, re-themed and reworked with original CC0 assets and my own spin on it. LuaJ powers one sandboxed VM per computer while the Computed engine owns graph scheduling, safe Minecraft endpoints, persistence, networking, the editor, monitor rendering, and integrations.

Program format 3 stores one root graph and an embedded Lua definition library. Legacy graphs, Functions, Sections, JSON custom nodes, CMP1, and CMP2 are intentionally discarded or rejected without migration.

Runnable code examples live under docs/lua/examples in the repository.

docs.title: Building
docs.text:
Build and verify with:

./gradlew clean check build

docs.title: Using the Editor
docs.text: Right-click a computer to open its node editor. Shift-right-click instead opens the peripheral bay (disks). The editor saves automatically about once per second and again when you close it — there is no save button.

docs.title: The toolbar
docs.text:
Top of the screen, left to right:

Button What it does « / » Show or hide the Node Explorer sidebar. Undo / Redo Step through up to 256 history states. Fit Zoom to fit the selection, or the whole graph (F). Docs Open the in-game documentation with 120+ importable examples. Import / Export Save and load graphs and nodes, set the computer ID and name. − / + Zoom out and in.

The bottom-left corner shows the computer's ID (also used for networking and shared package folders).

docs.title: Adding nodes
docs.text:
• Tab opens the quick-add picker at your cursor. Type to filter, arrow keys to choose, Enter to place it.
  • Shift+A opens the Node Explorer at your cursor.
  • Right-click the empty canvas → Open Node Explorer or New Lua Node….
  • Drag a wire from an output pin and drop it on empty canvas: the picker opens pre-filtered to nodes that accept that value type, and wires itself automatically.

docs.title: Selecting and editing
docs.text: Action How Rubber-band selection Left-drag on empty canvas (hold Shift to add to the selection) Move nodes Left-drag a node; dragging a frame moves everything inside it Copy / cut / paste Ctrl+C / Ctrl+X / Ctrl+V (paste lands at the cursor) Duplicate Ctrl+D (repeated presses form a ladder down-right) Unlink selected nodes Ctrl+U Delete Delete Select everything Ctrl+A Pan Middle- or right-drag

docs.title: Navigation
docs.text:
• Mouse wheel zooms around the cursor (10% – 300%).
  • F zooms to fit the selection, or the whole graph.
  • Double-click a node to zoom to it.
  • The minimap (bottom right) shows the whole graph — click or drag it to jump around.

docs.title: Undo and redo
docs.text: Ctrl+Z undoes, Ctrl+Y redoes (matched to your keyboard layout, so Ctrl+Z works on QWERTZ). Every layout operation — align, auto layout, frame moves — can be undone. Undoing back to the last saved state marks the graph as clean again.

docs.title: Frames and comments
docs.text:
Right-click the canvas:

  • Add Frame groups nodes visually. Drag a frame to move everything inside it. Right-click a frame for Select Frame Contents and five accent colors (Frame Color).
  • Add Comment places a text note above the graph. Double-click it to edit (up to 2000 characters).

Frames and comments never execute and are ignored by align and auto layout.

docs.title: Align and auto layout
docs.text:
Select two or more nodes, right-click → Align ▸: left, center, right, top, middle, bottom. With three or more nodes you also get Distribute H and Distribute V for even gaps.

Auto Layout (same menu) arranges nodes in topological columns from left to right. With a selection of two or more nodes it only touches the selection; otherwise it arranges the whole graph.

docs.title: Computer ID and name
docs.text: Import / Export → Set Computer ID assigns a numeric ID (shared package folders and network messaging use it). Set Computer Name gives the computer a display name (up to 32 characters) that shows in the editor, on portable monitor tabs, and for anyone linked to it.

docs.title: All keyboard shortcuts
docs.text:
The same list is available in-game as the Keyboard Shortcuts page in the Docs screen.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This tutorial builds your first program: a monitor that shows the world time. It takes about five minutes and needs no Lua knowledge.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Computer:

  • A Monitor block in front of the computer (the computer recipe needs one anyway).

Place the monitor first, then place the computer directly behind it so the monitor touches one of the computer's sides.

docs.title: Step 1 — Open the editor
docs.text: Right-click the computer. The node editor opens. This is where you wire nodes together. Everything is saved automatically — there is no save button.

docs.title: Step 2 — Add three nodes
docs.text:
Press Tab (or right-click the empty canvas) to open the node picker. Type a few letters, press Enter to place the node. Repeat for all three:

Find this node Why World Time Reads the time of day as a number (0–24000). Number Widget Displays a number on a monitor. Monitor Sends widgets to the monitor block in front of the computer.

Drag the nodes somewhere sensible. F zooms to fit everything.

docs.title: Step 3 — Connect them
docs.text:
Drag from a node's output pin (right side) to another node's input pin (left side):

  1. World Time time → Number Widget value
  2. Number Widget widget → Monitor widget_1

Widgets travel through the widget_1 input. The Monitor node has 16 of them (widget_1 … widget_16) — press + on the node to add more, − to remove the last one.

docs.title: Step 4 — See the result
docs.text:
Close the editor (ESC). The computer saves your graph on its own. The monitor in front of the computer now shows the world time, updating all day.

Something wrong?

Press F in the editor to see the whole graph. Check that every wire runs from a right-side pin to a left-side pin. The Monitor node's Face field must match the side the monitor is on (default: front).

docs.title: Computed Glasses
docs.text: The glasses are a wearable HUD (added in 1.2.7). Wear them on your head and they show a status line for your linked computer — plus up to 16 live widgets from your graph, right in the world.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The glasses carry no binding of their own. They mirror the first bound Link Card they find on you — main inventory first, then the offhand. Right-click a computer with a Link Card to bind it, then put the card anywhere in your inventory and wear the glasses.

You now see a line like Connected with: Base (or the computer's x/y/z when it has no name). Anyone linked to the same computer — drone pilot, plane crew, base operator — sees the same widgets on their glasses.

docs.title: Showing graph widgets on the glasses
docs.text:
Use the Glasses HUD node (Widgets category) exactly like a Monitor node: it has 16 widget inputs (widget_1 … widget_16), + adds one, − removes the last. Wire any widget nodes into it — text, numbers, buttons, progress bars — and every player wearing glasses linked to this computer sees them.

Line-layout widgets hug their content on the glasses — a short label stays a short label instead of stretching across the whole HUD. Set a widget's Fit field to fill when you want a full-width row.

docs.title: Adjusting the HUD (press K)
docs.text:
With the glasses equipped, press K to enter edit mode:

  • Double-click empty space to add a new HUD line.
  • Drag a line to move it, use the handle to resize, double-click to edit its text, color, and scale.
  • The Graph widgets box moves and rescales the whole widget region.
  • Save when you are done; ESC cancels.

Every HUD line is a text template. Available placeholders:

Placeholder Replaced with {computer} Computer name, or its position when unnamed {x} {y} {z} Computer coordinates {dimension} Dimension ID

Positions and scales are stored per element (normalized 0–1, so they survive resolution and GUI scale changes) in config/computed-glasses-hud.json.

docs.title: Ideas & Roadmap
docs.text:
This page collects what is planned for Winnie's Computed — and it is a thread you can write in. Everything here starts as a community idea.

Have an idea?

Open a post in the Ideas discussion thread on GitHub. Reply to existing posts to vote with a 👍, or start your own — a short title and one or two sentences are enough. The best ideas get picked up here.

docs.title: Open ideas
docs.text: Ideas the community and the maintainer still want to build. Click through to the thread if you want to comment on one.

docs.title: Speaker and audio
docs.text: • Custom instrument samples — drop your own .ogg files into the speaker folder to use them as instruments and waveforms.

docs.title: Widgets and display
docs.text:
• Chart widget — plot values over time as a curve (progress bar, checkbox, and text input already exist).
  • Image widget — show a texture or item icon on the monitor.
  • Right-click widget actions — a second action column for widgets (for example a context menu).

docs.title: Computer and world
docs.text:
• Radar / sensor endpoint — query entities, light level, weather, or blocks in a radius (scan(radius) returns a table).
  • Energy endpoint — read and extract FE/EU (Create / Forge Energy integration).

docs.title: Integrations
docs.text: • Create screens as monitors — bind Create's display blocks as a monitor surface (kinetic speed and stress already work through the Create Kinetic node).

docs.title: Recently shipped
docs.text:
A short look at what the thread already produced:

  • Speaker: Play Sequence (timed instrument:note:seconds melodies without clock nodes) and a disc playlist — queue up to 8 discs with right-click, play advances through them, loop cycles the whole queue.
  • Autostart disk — right-click a written Program Disk to flag it; the computer loads and runs the program at startup or as soon as the flagged disk is inserted (through the regular validation, an existing program always wins).
  • has_display() — computed:monitor/has_display and the Display Present node answer whether a wall monitor is attached at a face or a player carries a paired portable monitor.
  • Redstone endpoints — computed:redstone reads input/comparator levels and writes output at the computer's faces (Redstone Input, Comparator Read, Redstone Emitter nodes).
  • Speaker: Play Sweep (frequency glide), attack/decay envelopes on Play Wave, and disc loop for endless playback.
  • Aeronautics: vertical speed and altitude nodes, plus the Threshold Trigger node for alarms (altitude below X, overspeed, climb warnings).
  • Glasses HUD: graph widgets on your glasses, a movable widget region in the K designer, and a reworked glasses model with its own recipe.
  • Undo/redo and auto-save in the editor, the Lua live preview, and a demo disk in the creative tab.
  • Portable monitor: right-click a channel tab to remove it, and tabs show computer names.
  • Computer-to-computer messaging (computed:net), the Aeronautics telemetry nodes, and the Create Kinetic sensor.

Raw backlog

The maintainer's working list lives in IDEAS.md in the repository — the thread is the place to add to it.

docs.title: In-Game Documentation and Examples
docs.text: Computed ships its documentation inside the game. The Docs screen describes every bundled node and lets you import ready-made example programs with one click.

docs.title: Opening the Docs screen
docs.text: Open any computer's editor and press the Docs button in the toolbar (top right). There is no keybind or command.

docs.title: What you see
docs.text:
• Left column: every node grouped in folders (Math, Widgets, Logic, Speaker, Integration, …). Type in the search box to filter by title, ID, or description.
  • Right column: the selected node's description, its inputs and outputs, and a Lua example.
  • ↑ / ↓ jump between entries, ESC closes the screen.

Two extra pages live under Help:

  • How to use these docs — a short introduction.
  • Keyboard Shortcuts — the full editor shortcut list (also on the Using the Editor page).

docs.title: Importing an example
docs.text:
Select any node and press Import example (or No example if that node has none). The example graph is placed into the editor canvas of the computer you have open, fully wired and ready to run. From there it works like any other graph: edit it, extend it, save it to a program disk, or copy single nodes out of it.

Every bundled node has an example — there are over 120 of them, including examples for the integration nodes when the matching mod is installed.

Import replaces the canvas

Importing replaces the current graph on the canvas. Export or save your work first if you want to keep it. The usual limits apply (4096 nodes, 20000 connections, 4 MB per program).

docs.title: Integrations
docs.text: Computed talks to other mods through optional integrations. Only NeoForge and Minecraft are required — every integration activates on its own when the matching mod is installed.

docs.title: CC:Tweaked
docs.text: Full two-way support: call adjacent peripherals from Lua, exchange named channel values, and use Computed as a CC peripheral. See CC:Tweaked Integration for the details and the two bundled nodes (cc_input, cc_output).

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
Node Does Create Kinetic Reads speed, stress, and stress capacity of the Create block on a chosen face Create Link Sender Transmits on a Create redstone link (two item filters, power 0–15) Create Link Receiver Receives power from a Create redstone link

All three need an adjacent Create block or an available redstone-link network.

docs.title: Create Aeronautics
docs.text:
When Create Aeronautics is installed, Computed measures the nearest contraption (including flying structures) around the computer — 17 ready-made nodes from Aeronautics Telemetry (everything at once) down to single values like speed, vertical speed, altitude, heading, or pitch. Each node has a Face field; the measurement runs once per computer per tick no matter how many nodes you use.

Combine a scalar node with the Threshold Trigger node for alarms: altitude below 50 switches a speaker on, vertical speed above zero tells you you are climbing. The same data is available on the CC:Tweaked side as the peripheral method measure().

Sable Companion (optional) is supported: Create Aeronautics uses it for hidden physics sublevels, and Computed reads contraption positions through it automatically.

docs.title: Jade and WTHIT
docs.text: Hover a Computed computer with Jade or WTHIT installed and the tooltip shows the computer's ID — handy when you wire up networking between machines.

docs.title: Monitors
docs.text: Monitors are blocks that show your graph's widgets: text, buttons, tables, terminals, and more. A monitor block grows automatically into a bigger screen when you place more monitors next to it.

docs.title: Crafting and placing a monitor
docs.text: Where you look while placing decides the orientation: look straight ahead for a wall screen, look down for a floor screen, look up for a ceiling screen.

docs.title: Growing the screen
docs.text: Place another monitor block directly next to an existing screen (same orientation) and the two merge into one bigger screen, up to 8 blocks wide and 6 blocks high. Breaking a block of a bigger screen splits the rest into new screens.

docs.title: Connecting a screen to a computer
docs.text:
Place the screen so it touches one side of the computer, then use a Monitor node in your graph. Its Face field selects the side (front by default — set it to the side the screen is on).

The Monitor node collects up to 16 widgets through its widget_1 … widget_16 inputs and sends them to the screen. Press + on the node to add an input, − to remove the last one.

Screen goes blank?

The computer must run a graph tick that feeds the Monitor node. If the graph stops (or the computer is removed), the screen clears after a moment.

docs.title: Widget layout
docs.text:
Every widget node has a Layout field with two modes:

  • line (default): the widget takes a full row. Line picks the row (1 = top), Span makes it taller (for example a table with span 4). If the chosen row is occupied, the widget moves to the next free row.
  • manual: you set X, Y, Width, and Height in pixels yourself for free positioning.

A 1-block screen is 64×64 pixels (2 rows); the biggest 8×6 screen is 512×384 pixels (12 rows). Two widgets that end up on the same spot in line mode — the later one is dropped.

docs.title: The widget types
docs.text: Widget node Shows Text Widget One line of text Number Widget A right-aligned number Clock Widget Current time, optional seconds Text Block Multiple lines of text Button Clickable label (sends an event to the node) Checkbox Toggle (sends an event to the node) Slider Value between min and max Number Input Editable number (click opens a dialog) Text Input Editable text (click opens a dialog, up to 256 characters) Progress Bar Value as a bar Panel Background rectangle Table Header plus rows (up to 16 columns × 64 rows) Terminal Terminal area (64 lines × 256 characters) Terminal Line One styled terminal line

docs.title: Clicking widgets
docs.text: Buttons, checkboxes, sliders, and text inputs react to clicks on the screen (within 16 blocks of the computer). Clicks are forwarded to the widget nodes as events — see Graph Events.

docs.title: Portable screens
docs.text: The Portable Monitor item shows the same widgets on a handheld 16:9 screen without placing any monitor blocks.

docs.title: Portable Monitor and Link Card
docs.text: The Portable Monitor is a handheld screen. It streams the widget output of up to 8 computers without placing any monitor blocks — useful for drones, planes, or just checking your base from your inventory.

docs.title: Crafting
docs.text:
Link Card — one row: paper, copper, redstone.

Portable Monitor — a shaped recipe: iron in the four corners, glass in the middle column, redstone left and right of the glass, link card on top.

docs.title: Linking computers
docs.text:
• Right-click a computer with the Portable Monitor to add it as a channel. Right-click more computers to add more channels (up to 8; the same computer is never stored twice).
  • Shift-right-click a computer to remove that computer from the channel list again.
  • Shift-right-click in the air to clear all channels.

The item glows once it stores at least one channel, and its tooltip shows the linked position.

docs.title: Using the screen
docs.text:
Right-click in the air to open the display. It shows the widgets of the active channel exactly like a wall monitor would — buttons, sliders, and text inputs are clickable.

  • Click a channel tab (or press arrow left/right) to switch computers.
  • Right-click a channel tab to remove that channel.
  • ESC closes the screen; the game keeps running.

If the screen says no signal, the linked computer is probably not running a graph that feeds a Monitor node — see Monitors.

Same widgets, smaller screen

The portable canvas is 256×144 pixels with 6 rows, while a wall monitor starts at 64×64 pixels per block. All 12 widget types work on both.

docs.title: Link Cards
docs.text:
A Link Card stores a reference to one computer:

  • Right-click a computer to bind the card to it (the card glows and shows the position).
  • Shift-right-click in the air to clear the binding.

Link cards have two uses:

  1. Copy a link: hold a bound card in your offhand and shift-right-click the air while holding the Portable Monitor — the monitor replaces all its channels with just this one computer.
  2. Authorization: anyone carrying a bound Link Card (in the inventory or offhand) can view and click the linked computer's displays, even from far away — there is no distance limit. This is what keeps drones and planes usable.

Computed Glasses use the same trick: they mirror your first bound card as a wearable HUD.

docs.title: Limits at a glance
docs.text: Limit Value Channels per monitor 8 Screen 256×144 px, 6 rows Update rate About every 0.75 seconds, only when the picture changes Widget clicks Forwarded to the computer (buttons, sliders, text inputs)

docs.title: Speaker
docs.text: The Speaker block plays notes, sounds, generated waves, and music discs from your graph. Place up to six speakers around one computer — one per side.

docs.title: Crafting
docs.text: The speaker faces you when you place it. Right-click it with a music disc to insert the disc; right-click it empty-handed to take discs back — the inserted one first, then one queued disc per click. Breaking the speaker drops the inserted disc and the whole queue.

docs.title: Addressing a speaker
docs.text: Every speaker node has a Face field (front by default). It selects the side of the computer the speaker sits on: front, back, left, right, up, down (also north, east, south, west, top, bottom). The node errors if no speaker is on that side.

docs.title: The nine speaker nodes
docs.text:
Eight of them are triggers: they run when their Trigger input turns on or an event arrives.

Node What it does Extra fields Play Note Plays one note-block note Instrument (16 choices, default harp), Note 0–24 (default 12) Play Sound Plays any named sound Sound ID (e.g. block.note_block.pling), Volume 0–4, Pitch 0.5–2 Play Wave Plays a synthesized waveform Wave (sine, square, saw, triangle, noise), Frequency 55–3520 Hz, Volume 0–3, Attack 0–2 s, Decay 0–2 s Play Sweep Glides between two frequencies Wave, From/To 55–3520 Hz, Duration 0.2–10 s, Volume Play Disc Starts the inserted music disc Loop (restarts the disc at song end) Play Sequence Plays timed notes without a disc Notes 1–16 (text steps like harp:12:0.5) Stop Stops whatever is playing — Eject Spits the disc out — Speaker Status Reports the speaker state Outputs: has_disc, is_playing, is_looping, queued (updates every tick)

Example — play a doorbell note when a button is pressed:

  1. Place a Play Note node, set Instrument to bell and Note to 18.
  2. Connect a button widget (or any boolean source) to Trigger.
  3. Set Face to the side the speaker is on.

Example — an alarm that alternates two notes: drive Trigger from a fast counter or pulse node and switch the note with an if branch.

docs.title: Disc playlist
docs.text:
Right-click a speaker with a music disc to queue it behind the inserted one — up to 8 discs wait in the playlist (Speaker Status reports them as queued).

  • Play Disc starts the inserted disc; with the slot empty it pulls the first queued disc.
  • When a song ends and discs are queued, the finished disc drops on the ground like a vanilla jukebox and the next queued disc starts.
  • With Loop on, the playlist cycles: the finished disc joins the queue's end and the next one starts, forever.
  • Empty-hand clicks and Eject remove the inserted disc first, then one queued disc per click — every disc stays reachable without playing the playlist through.

docs.title: Note sequences
docs.text:
Play Sequence plays a little melody with its own timing — no disc, no clock nodes. Fill the Notes inputs with instrument:note:seconds steps, top to bottom; empty inputs are skipped. The seconds value after a note is the gap until the next one:

note_1: harp:12:0.5
note_2: bell:18:0.5
note_3: pling:15:0.5

plays three notes, half a second apart. Trigger (or an event) starts the sequence; Stop cancels a running one. Instruments and note range are the same as Play Note; each gap is 0–10 s. The underlying endpoint accepts up to 64 notes for custom node setups.

docs.title: Envelopes, sweeps, and loops
docs.text:
• Attack / decay on Play Wave fade a tone in and out so notes do not cut off harshly. The envelope restarts the tone in short slices, so keep attack/decay at a few tenths of a second for the smoothest result.
  • Play Sweep glides linearly from one frequency to another — risers, alarms, motors.
  • Loop on Play Disc restarts the disc automatically when the song ends — with a playlist queued, it cycles through the discs instead. The toggle applies immediately, even while a song is playing, and survives world saves. Turn it off (or hit Stop) to end playback; the Speaker Status node reports is_looping.

One tone per speaker

Envelope slices and sweeps cut the previous slice before restarting, so overlapping wave tones on the same speaker (or the same waveform on several speakers) may cut each other. For polyphony, use one speaker per voice.

docs.title: Useful limits
docs.text:
Limit Value Note range 0–24 (12 = A, the default) Note instruments harp, basedrum, snare, hat, bass, flute, bell, guitar, chime, xylophone, iron_xylophone, cow_bell, didgeridoo, bit, banjo, pling Wave frequencies 55–3520 Hz Wave aliases sin→sine, sq→square, sawtooth→saw, tri→triangle, white→noise Envelope range Attack/decay 0–2 s each Sweep range 0.2–10 s, sliced every 0.1 s Simultaneous discs One inserted + 8 queued (playlist) Sequence Node: 16 note inputs; endpoint: up to 64 notes, gaps 0–10 s each Speakers per computer Six (one per side)

Timing is up to your graph: speaker nodes have no built-in wait — use a Delay node, drive them from a tick-based counter, or let Play Sequence handle the timing itself.

docs.title: Architecture and Package Boundaries
docs.text:
• graph owns immutable graphs, stable ports, deterministic analysis, and scheduling.
  • lua/compiler owns validation, SHA-256 hashing, and prototype caching.
  • lua/runtime owns per-computer VMs, transactional node instances, coroutines, and state serialization.
  • lua/sandbox owns globals and instruction budgets.
  • lua/node owns schemas, the fluent contract, bundled definitions, and embedded libraries.
  • lua/endpoint owns safe Java registrations and preview fixtures.
  • client/editor owns explorer and focused editor state.
  • client/renderer/node owns the semantic palette and shared layout.
  • persistence owns format 3 and the clean legacy reset.
  • network remains authoritative for distance, permissions, revisions, and payload size.
  • integration/computercraft, integration/create, integration/aeronautics, integration/jade, and integration/wthit own optional API boundaries and lifecycle cleanup.

Minecraft and addon objects stop at endpoint handlers. Lua nodes communicate through scheduler-owned edges, never by directly calling neighbors. WireEditorController remains the unchanged compatibility boundary for curves, colors, thickness, pulses, waypoints, hit testing, and socket behavior.

Format 3 stores one root graph, an embedded Lua library, definition ID/hash references, stable port snapshots, persistent state, revision, and metadata. It stores no Functions or Sections.

docs.title: Lua Node Authoring Guide
docs.text:
New to Computed? The Getting Started tutorial shows the editor basics first. This page is about writing your own nodes in Lua.

Every Computed node is a Lua definition. A file creates one node, declares an immutable schema, installs callbacks, and returns that node.

local node = computed.node(1, "example:counter", "Counter")

node:category("state")
node:style("standard")
node:input("increment", "number")
node:output("count", "number")
node:field("step", "number", {
    default = 1,
    min = 0,
    max = 10,
    control = "slider",
    step = 0.5,
    label = "Step Size"
})
node:state("count", 0)

node:on_run(function(ctx)
    local next = ctx:state("count") + ctx:input("increment") * ctx:field("step")
    ctx:set_state("count", next)
    ctx:output("count", next)
end)

return node

Definition IDs are stable, lowercase, namespaced identifiers. Port, field, state, and event IDs start with a lowercase letter and contain only lowercase letters, digits, _, ., or -. Schemas cannot change while an instance is running.

Choose input execution for dataflow nodes, tick for world sensors, step for explicitly stepped nodes, and event when only named handlers should run. A failed invocation discards all staged output and state changes. The next eligible execution retries the callback.

For user-authored wireless graph flow, see Graph events. Lua callbacks can inspect configurable per-instance inputs with ctx:inputs().

Use endpoints for Minecraft or addon access. Lua values never contain Java or Minecraft objects.

docs.title: Create a node in a computer
docs.text:
Open the Node Explorer, expand User Nodes, and choose New Lua Node…. The editor starts with a unique reusable user:node_<id> definition. Edit and preview the source, then choose Save. Computed adds the validated definition to that computer's embedded library and places its first instance at the canvas anchor. Additional instances appear under User Nodes and can be placed like bundled nodes.

Right-click an existing definition in the explorer to edit it. Replacing a definition with the same ID requires confirmation when its source hash changes.

docs.title: Field controls
docs.text:
Field values belong to each node instance and participate in autosave, undo, duplication, and server validation. Use value controls for unrestricted numbers and explicit sliders for bounded values:

node:field("name", "text", { default = "Display" })
node:field("enabled", "boolean", { default = true })
node:field("side", "direction", { default = "front" })
node:field("mode", "choice", {
    default = "normal",
    choices = { "normal", "inverted" }
})
node:field("speed", "number", {
    default = 10,
    min = 0,
    max = 20,
    control = "slider",
    step = 1
})

See Lua API Reference, Types and State, Sandbox and Budgets, and the examples in the repository.

docs.title: CC:Tweaked Integration
docs.text:
CC:Tweaked support is optional and targets its public dan200.computercraft.api surface. It is peripheral interoperability, not CraftOS compatibility.

Adjacent peripherals are exposed through ctx:endpoint("computercraft:peripheral", side). A proxy provides methods() and call(methodName, ...). Calls return an integer-keyed result table. Main-thread tasks and yielded MethodResult continuations suspend the node while committed outputs remain visible. Queued peripheral events resume pull-event callbacks. Unload, definition replacement, peripheral detach, or cancellation terminates the continuation safely.

Dedicated CC Input and CC Output Lua nodes exchange named channel values. The Computed peripheral lists channels, reads outputs, writes inputs, and emits output-changed events.

When Create Aeronautics is installed, the peripheral also exposes a fixed measure() method. It returns the same telemetry table as the aeronautics:telemetry endpoint (position, velocity, speed, heading, and the rest).

Filesystem, terminal, rednet, HTTP, and other CraftOS globals are not exposed.

local node = computed.node(1, "example:cc_query", "CC Query")
node:field("side", "direction", { default = "left" })
node:output("result", "table")
node:on_run(function(ctx)
    local peripheral = ctx:endpoint("computercraft:peripheral", ctx:field("side"))
    ctx:output("result", { methods = peripheral:methods() })
end)
return node

docs.title: Calling an adjacent peripheral
docs.text:
local node = computed.node(1, "example:cc_call", "CC Call")
node:category("integration/computercraft")
node:execution("tick")
node:field("side", "direction", { default = "left" })
node:output("result", "table")
node:on_run(function(ctx)
    local peripheral = ctx:endpoint("computercraft:peripheral", ctx:field("side"))
    ctx:output("result", peripheral:call("getEnergy"))
end)
return node

If getEnergy completes immediately, the result table is committed in the same graph tick. If it returns a yielding MethodResult, the invocation remains private until its callback completes. The prior committed output remains visible while waiting.

docs.title: Using Computed channels from CraftOS
docs.text:
local computed = peripheral.find("computed")
computed.write("control", { enabled = true, level = 12 })

for _, name in ipairs(computed.listChannels()) do
    print(name)
end

local status = computed.read("status")
local event, channel, value = os.pullEvent("computed_output_changed")

write(channel, value) feeds a CC Input node. read(channel) reads the latest CC Output value. listChannels() returns input and output channel names. computed_output_changed is queued only when a published value changes.

docs.title: Yielded call behavior
docs.text: Only values supported by both Computed state serialization and the CC API cross the bridge: nil, booleans, finite numbers, strings, and acyclic tables with string or integer keys. Filesystem mounts are refused. A detached peripheral fails its pending invocation, releases its attachment, and leaves committed state and outputs unchanged.

docs.title: Java Endpoint API
docs.text: Endpoints are the only bridge from Lua to Minecraft and addons. Handlers receive the host object; Lua receives only validated values.

docs.title: ComputedEndpoints.register(id, registration)
docs.text:
Registers one stable namespaced endpoint during mod setup and returns its immutable definition. The registration callback receives an EndpointBuilder. It runs on the registration thread, is unavailable to Lua previews, and has the side effect of adding a global API entry. It throws on invalid or duplicate endpoint IDs.

ComputedEndpoints.register("addon:storage", endpoint -> endpoint
        .method("stored", signature, policy, handler, previewFixture, "Returns stored units."));

docs.title: EndpointBuilder.method(methodId, signature, policy, handler)
docs.text: Adds a method and returns the builder. Parameters declare stable ID, argument/return schema, execution/yield/side-effect/preview policy, and handler. The short overload marks preview unavailable. It throws on duplicate IDs or incomplete preview policy.

docs.title: EndpointBuilder.method(methodId, signature, policy, handler, previewFixture, documentation)
docs.text: Adds a fully described method and returns the builder. previewFixture must be deterministic when preview is enabled. The documentation string feeds completion/signature help. Handler side effects must match the policy.

docs.title: ComputedEndpoints.find(id)
docs.text: Returns an optional immutable endpoint definition. It has no side effects and may be called on either side for metadata lookup.

docs.title: ComputedEndpoints.definitions()
docs.text: Returns all definitions sorted by stable ID. It has no side effects and powers documentation/completion checks.

docs.title: EndpointSignature.of(arguments, returns)
docs.text: Creates a fixed-arity signature from ordered argument and return type lists. Empty lists mean no arguments or no returns. It returns an immutable signature, runs during registration on either side, has no preview behavior or side effects, and rejects no values beyond null lists becoming empty. Use the three-argument EndpointSignature constructor with variadic = true when trailing values are allowed. Example: EndpointSignature.of(List.of(EndpointType.STRING), List.of(EndpointType.NUMBER)).

docs.title: EndpointPolicy.computerThread(sideEffect, previewAvailable)
docs.text: Creates a non-yielding computer-thread policy. sideEffect declares production mutation and previewAvailable requires a deterministic fixture. It returns an immutable policy, runs during registration, and has no side effect itself. Use the record constructor for server-thread or yielding methods. Example: EndpointPolicy.computerThread(false, true).

docs.title: EndpointResult.immediate(values...)
docs.text: Returns validated Lua values without suspending the node. Parameters are zero or more LuaJ values; the default is no values. It can be returned on either execution side, has no side effect itself, and is used unchanged by preview fixtures. Return-schema mismatches become runtime errors. Example: return EndpointResult.immediate(LuaValue.valueOf(12));.

docs.title: EndpointResult.yielded(continuation)
docs.text: Suspends the current node until the completion stage supplies an immediate result. The continuation is required and the endpoint policy must declare yielding. It is unavailable in preview unless a separate immediate fixture exists. Cancellation, exceptional completion, unload, definition replacement, or detach fails the invocation while retaining prior committed outputs. Example: return EndpointResult.yielded(future);.

docs.title: EndpointResult.unavailable(reason)
docs.text: Returns an explicit unavailable result with a nonblank reason. Calling Lua receives a runtime error; no values or side effects are produced. It is suitable for optional integrations and blocked preview behavior. Example: return EndpointResult.unavailable("machine is not loaded");.

docs.title: EndpointRuntimeLifecycle.register(listener)
docs.text: Registers tick and unload callbacks for endpoint-owned external state. The listener is required for useful behavior and is called with the computer ID and host. Registration mutates the global lifecycle list, runs during mod setup, and has no preview callback. Listeners must cancel pending work and release addon objects on unload. Example: EndpointRuntimeLifecycle.register(listener);.

docs.title: computed:world/time
docs.text: Signature: () -> number. Runs on the server thread, does not yield, has no side effects, and returns fixture 6000 in preview. Errors when the computer host cannot expose world time. Example: ctx:endpoint("computed:world"):call("time").

docs.title: computed:world/position
docs.text: Signature: () -> number, number, number. Runs on the server thread, has no side effects, and is available in previews with a fixed position fixture. Errors when host world access is unavailable. Example: local x, y, z = ctx:endpoint("computed:world"):call("position").

docs.title: computed:world/rotation
docs.text: Signature: () -> number, number, number. Runs on the server thread, has no side effects, and is available in previews with a fixed rotation fixture. Errors when host world access is unavailable. Example: local yaw, pitch, roll = ctx:endpoint("computed:world"):call("rotation").

docs.title: computed:world/block_present
docs.text: Signature: (face: string) -> boolean. Runs on the server thread, has no side effects, and returns false in previews. Unknown face names return false; invalid argument types are errors. Example: ctx:endpoint("computed:world"):call("block_present", "front").

docs.title: computed:world/block_id
docs.text: Signature: (face: string) -> string. Runs on the server thread, has no side effects, and returns minecraft:air in previews. Unknown face names return minecraft:air; invalid argument types are errors. Example: ctx:endpoint("computed:world"):call("block_id", "front").

docs.title: computed:redstone/input
docs.text: Signature: (face: string) -> number. Runs on the server thread, has no side effects, and returns zero in previews. Unknown face names return zero. Example: ctx:endpoint("computed:redstone"):call("input", "left").

docs.title: computed:redstone/comparator
docs.text: Signature: (face: string) -> number. Runs on the server thread, has no side effects, and returns zero in previews. Unknown face names return zero. Example: ctx:endpoint("computed:redstone"):call("comparator", "front").

docs.title: computed:redstone/output
docs.text: Signature: (face: string, level: number) -> (). Runs on the server thread, clamps power to 0–15, performs a world side effect, and is unavailable in previews. Unknown face names are ignored. Example: ctx:endpoint("computed:redstone"):call("output", "back", 15).

docs.title: computed:command/run
docs.text: Signature: (string) -> (). Runs on the server thread, performs a command side effect, and is unavailable in preview. The Creative Computer type no longer exists, so this endpoint currently errors on every computer; it stays registered for compatibility. Example: ctx:endpoint("computed:command"):call("run", "say hello").

docs.title: computed:widget/text
docs.text: Signature: (text: string, color: number) -> table. Runs on the computer thread, does not yield, has no world side effect, and uses the same deterministic fixture in preview. Returns a full text widget table. Example: ctx:output("widget", ctx:endpoint("computed:widget"):call("text", "Ready", 0xffffffff)).

docs.title: computed:widget/number
docs.text: Signature: (value: number, text: string, color: number) -> table. Runs on the computer thread, has no side effects, and has a deterministic preview fixture. Renders the preformatted text right-aligned; value is carried for semantics. Format the text node-side with string.format. Example: ctx:output("widget", ctx:endpoint("computed:widget"):call("number", 3.14159, "3.1416", 0xffffffff)).

docs.title: computed:widget/clock
docs.text: Signature: (color: number, showSeconds: boolean) -> table. Runs on the computer thread, has no side effects, and has a deterministic preview fixture. Errors on invalid argument types. Example: ctx:endpoint("computed:widget"):call("clock", 0xffffffff, true).

docs.title: computed:widget/button
docs.text: Signature: (label: string, color: number) -> table. Runs on the computer thread, has no side effects, and has a deterministic preview fixture. The returned table carries the node instance ID for targeted input events. Example: ctx:endpoint("computed:widget"):call("button", "Run", 0xffffffff).

docs.title: computed:widget/checkbox
docs.text: Signature: (label: string, color: number, checked: boolean) -> table. Runs on the computer thread, has no side effects, and has a deterministic preview fixture. Clicks on the rendered widget deliver a toggle input event to the originating node; the node owns the checked state. Example: ctx:endpoint("computed:widget"):call("checkbox", "Enabled", 0xffffffff, false).

docs.title: computed:widget/text_input
docs.text: Signature: (placeholder: string, color: number, value: string) -> table. Runs on the computer thread, has no side effects, and has a deterministic preview fixture. Clicking the widget opens a client-side text dialog; the submitted string is routed to the node's input event. Example: ctx:endpoint("computed:widget"):call("text_input", "Name…", 0xffffffff, "").

docs.title: computed:widget/slider
docs.text: Signature: (value: number, minimum: number, maximum: number, color: number, step: number) -> table. Runs on the computer thread, has no side effects, and has a deterministic preview fixture. Errors on invalid argument types. Example: ctx:endpoint("computed:widget"):call("slider", 0.5, 0, 1, 0xffffffff, 0.01).

docs.title: computed:widget/progress
docs.text: Signature: (value: number, maximum: number, color: number, segments: number) -> table. Runs on the computer thread, has no side effects, and has a deterministic preview fixture. Errors on invalid argument types. Example: ctx:endpoint("computed:widget"):call("progress", 5, 10, 0xffffffff, 10).

docs.title: computed:widget/terminal
docs.text: Signature: (rows: table, fg: number, bg: number, scale: number, cursorX: number, cursorY: number) -> table. Runs on the computer thread, has no side effects, and has a deterministic preview fixture. rows is an array of strings or styled row tables from computed:widget/line; at most 64 rows are kept and each row is clipped to 256 characters. fg/bg are default ARGB colors, scale is clamped to 0.5–2, and cursorX/cursorY hide the cursor when negative. Example: ctx:endpoint("computed:widget"):call("terminal", {"Ready"}, 0xffffffff, 0xff000000, 1, -1, -1).

docs.title: computed:widget/line
docs.text: Signature: (text: string, fg: number, bg: number) -> table. Runs on the computer thread, has no side effects, and has a deterministic preview fixture. Returns a styled terminal row table usable in a computed:widget/terminal rows array. Example: ctx:endpoint("computed:widget"):call("line", "OK", 0xff00ff00, 0xff000000).

docs.title: computed:widget/panel
docs.text: Signature: (color: number, border: number) -> table. Runs on the computer thread, has no side effects, and has a deterministic preview fixture. Returns a panel widget; border of 0 draws no border. Example: ctx:endpoint("computed:widget"):call("panel", 0xff3c3c3c, 0).

docs.title: computed:widget/text_block
docs.text: Signature: (text: string, fg: number, bg: number, alignment: string) -> table. Runs on the computer thread, has no side effects, and has a deterministic preview fixture. Returns a multiline text block widget; lines are separated by \n and bg of 0 is transparent. Example: ctx:endpoint("computed:widget"):call("text_block", "line 1\nline 2", 0xffffffff, 0, "left").

docs.title: computed:widget/table
docs.text: Signature: (columns: string, rows: table, headerFg: number, headerBg: number, cellFg: number, cellBg: number) -> table. Runs on the computer thread, has no side effects, and has a deterministic preview fixture. columns is a comma-separated header list; rows is an array of comma-separated strings or arrays of cell strings. At most 16 columns and 64 rows of 64 characters are kept. Example: ctx:endpoint("computed:widget"):call("table", "Name,Value", {"a,1", "b,2"}, 0xffffffff, 0xff202020, 0xffffffff, 0xff000000).

docs.title: computed:monitor/show
docs.text: Signature: (widgets: table) -> (). Runs on the server thread, refreshes an adjacent monitor, performs a world side effect, and is unavailable in previews. The endpoint target selects the computer-relative face. Invalid widget records are ignored. Example: ctx:endpoint("computed:monitor", "front"):call("show", widgets).

docs.title: computed:monitor/has_display
docs.text: Signature: () -> boolean. Reports whether a display answers this computer: a formed monitor multiblock at the endpoint target face, or a player carrying a portable monitor paired with this computer — so programs can check before showing widgets. Example: ctx:endpoint("computed:monitor", "front"):call("has_display").

docs.title: computed:glasses/show
docs.text: Signature: (widgets: table) -> (). Runs on the server thread, performs a world side effect, and is unavailable in previews. Shows widget values on the glasses HUD of every player whose link card points at this computer: widgets keep their own x/y and size like on a monitor, resolved onto the fixed glasses canvas, while HUD element positions and scale stay in the K designer. Invalid widget records are ignored. Example: ctx:endpoint("computed:glasses"):call("show", widgets).

docs.title: computed:fs/list
docs.text: Signature: (path: string) -> table. Lists entry names inside a directory on the per-computer isolated filesystem (rooted under the world save). Runs on the computer thread with a filesystem side effect and is unavailable in preview. Errors when the filesystem is not attached or the path is not a directory. Example: local names = ctx:endpoint("computed:fs"):call("list", "/").

docs.title: computed:fs/exists
docs.text: Signature: (path: string) -> boolean. Reports whether a path exists on the computer filesystem. Runs on the computer thread, does not yield, and is unavailable in preview. Errors when the filesystem is not attached. Example: local present = ctx:endpoint("computed:fs"):call("exists", "/config.txt").

docs.title: computed:fs/is_dir
docs.text: Signature: (path: string) -> boolean. Reports whether a path is a directory. Runs on the computer thread, does not yield, and is unavailable in preview. Errors when the filesystem is not attached. Example: local isFolder = ctx:endpoint("computed:fs"):call("is_dir", "/logs").

docs.title: computed:fs/is_read_only
docs.text: Signature: (path: string) -> boolean. Always returns false; the computer filesystem is writable within its quota. Runs on the computer thread and is unavailable in preview. Example: local locked = ctx:endpoint("computed:fs"):call("is_read_only", "/data.txt").

docs.title: computed:fs/get_size
docs.text: Signature: (path: string) -> number. Returns the size of a file in bytes. Runs on the computer thread and is unavailable in preview. Errors when the filesystem is not attached, the path is missing, or the path is a directory. Example: local bytes = ctx:endpoint("computed:fs"):call("get_size", "/data.txt").

docs.title: computed:fs/get_free_space
docs.text: Signature: (path: string) -> number. Returns remaining quota bytes for the computer filesystem (path is accepted for CraftOS compatibility and ignored). Runs on the computer thread and is unavailable in preview. Example: local free = ctx:endpoint("computed:fs"):call("get_free_space", "/").

docs.title: computed:fs/make_dir
docs.text: Signature: (path: string) -> boolean. Creates a directory and parents; succeeds when the directory already exists. Runs on the computer thread with a filesystem side effect and is unavailable in preview. Errors when the filesystem is not attached or the path is invalid. Example: ctx:endpoint("computed:fs"):call("make_dir", "/logs").

docs.title: computed:fs/move
docs.text: Signature: (from: string, to: string) -> boolean. Moves or renames a file within the computer filesystem. Runs on the computer thread with a filesystem side effect and is unavailable in preview. Errors when the source is missing, a directory, or the quota would be exceeded. Example: ctx:endpoint("computed:fs"):call("move", "/old.txt", "/new.txt").

docs.title: computed:fs/copy
docs.text: Signature: (from: string, to: string) -> boolean. Copies a file within the computer filesystem. Runs on the computer thread with a filesystem side effect and is unavailable in preview. Errors when the source is missing, a directory, or the quota would be exceeded. Example: ctx:endpoint("computed:fs"):call("copy", "/data.txt", "/backup.txt").

docs.title: computed:fs/delete
docs.text: Signature: (path: string) -> boolean. Deletes a file or directory tree. Missing paths succeed. Runs on the computer thread with a filesystem side effect and is unavailable in preview. Errors when the filesystem is not attached or the path is invalid. Example: ctx:endpoint("computed:fs"):call("delete", "/tmp.txt").

docs.title: computed:fs/combine
docs.text: Signature: (...) -> string. Joins path segments into a normalized computer path (variadic). Runs on the computer thread, has no side effects, and is unavailable in preview. Example: local path = ctx:endpoint("computed:fs"):call("combine", "/", "logs", "run.txt").

docs.title: computed:fs/get_dir
docs.text: Signature: (path: string) -> string. Returns the parent directory of a path. Runs on the computer thread, has no side effects, and is unavailable in preview. Example: local parent = ctx:endpoint("computed:fs"):call("get_dir", "/logs/run.txt").

docs.title: computed:fs/get_name
docs.text: Signature: (path: string) -> string. Returns the final segment of a path. Runs on the computer thread, has no side effects, and is unavailable in preview. Example: local name = ctx:endpoint("computed:fs"):call("get_name", "/logs/run.txt").

docs.title: computed:fs/get_id
docs.text: Signature: () -> number. Returns this computer's numeric id — the folder name under <world>/computed/computer/. Runs on the computer thread, has no side effects, and is unavailable in preview. Example: local id = ctx:endpoint("computed:fs"):call("get_id").

docs.title: computed:fs/open
docs.text: Signature: (path: string, mode: string) -> table. Opens a file with mode r, w, a, rb, wb, or ab and returns a handle table. Handle methods: read_line(), read_all(), read(count), read_bytes(count), write(text), write_line(text), seek(whence, offset), flush(), close(). Reads return nil at EOF. Runs on the computer thread with a filesystem side effect and is unavailable in preview. Errors on unsupported modes, missing read targets, closed handles, mode mismatches, or quota exhaustion. Example: local handle = ctx:endpoint("computed:fs"):call("open", "/note.txt", "w"); handle:write_line("hi"); handle:close().

docs.title: computed:net/send
docs.text: Signature: (target: number, message: string) -> boolean. Queues a message for the computer with that numeric ID (computers sharing an ID share the inbox). Messages are at most 1024 characters; 64 messages are kept per computer and the oldest are dropped when the queue is full. Returns true when the target computer was online, false when the message was only queued. Runs on the server thread with a side effect and is unavailable in preview. Errors on a negative target or an oversized message. Example: ctx:endpoint("computed:net"):call("send", 3, "ready").

docs.title: computed:net/broadcast
docs.text: Signature: (message: string) -> number. Queues the message for every online computer except the sender and returns how many were reached. The same size and queue limits as send apply. Runs on the server thread with a side effect and is unavailable in preview. Errors on an oversized message. Example: local reached = ctx:endpoint("computed:net"):call("broadcast", "ping").

docs.title: computed:net/receive
docs.text: Signature: (timeout: number) -> sender: number?, message: string?. Waits for the next queued message and returns the sender ID and the message, or nil values when the timeout in seconds elapses first (0 waits indefinitely). The node yields while waiting, so other nodes keep ticking. Messages are held for up to two minutes for computers that are offline or not listening. Runs on the server thread with a side effect and is unavailable in preview. Errors when the timeout is negative or above 600 seconds. Example: local sender, message = ctx:endpoint("computed:net"):call("receive", 5).

docs.title: create:kinetic/speed
docs.text: Signature: () -> number. The target is a computer-relative face. It runs on the computer/server tick thread, does not yield or mutate the world, and returns zero in preview. Production errors when Create is absent or the target is invalid; a non-kinetic block returns zero. Example: ctx:endpoint("create:kinetic", "front"):call("speed").

docs.title: create:kinetic/stress
docs.text: Signature: () -> number. It returns the adjacent Create block's applied stress units, runs on the computer/server tick thread, does not yield or mutate, and returns zero in preview. Missing Create and invalid targets are errors; non-kinetic blocks return zero. Example: ctx:endpoint("create:kinetic", "left"):call("stress").

docs.title: create:kinetic/capacity
docs.text: Signature: () -> number. It returns the adjacent Create block's generated stress capacity, runs on the computer/server tick thread, does not yield or mutate, and returns zero in preview. Missing Create and invalid targets are errors; non-kinetic blocks return zero. Example: ctx:endpoint("create:kinetic", "right"):call("capacity").

docs.title: create:redstone_link/receive
docs.text: Signature: (firstItemId: string, secondItemId: string) -> number. It registers a virtual Create redstone-link listener owned by the node and returns power from 0 through 15. It runs on the server tick thread, does not yield, retains an external network actor, and is unavailable in preview. Invalid item IDs, absent Create, or unavailable network APIs are errors or return zero. Actors are removed on definition replacement and unload. Example: ctx:endpoint("create:redstone_link"):call("receive", "minecraft:iron_ingot", "minecraft:redstone").

docs.title: create:redstone_link/transmit
docs.text: Signature: (firstItemId: string, secondItemId: string, strength: number) -> (). It registers or updates a virtual Create transmitter, clamps strength to 0 through 15, performs a network side effect, runs on the server tick thread, does not yield, and is unavailable in preview. Invalid items or absent Create fail the invocation. Actors are removed on definition replacement and unload. Example: ctx:endpoint("create:redstone_link"):call("transmit", "minecraft:iron_ingot", "minecraft:redstone", 15).

docs.title: computercraft:channel/read
docs.text: Signature: (channel: string) -> table. It returns { value = ... } for the named value written by an attached CC computer. Names contain 1 through 64 characters. It runs on the computer thread, does not yield or mutate the world, and returns an empty table fixture in preview. It errors when CC is absent or the host is not a server computer. Example: ctx:endpoint("computercraft:channel"):call("read", "control").

docs.title: computercraft:channel/publish
docs.text: Signature: (channel: string, value: table) -> (). It publishes a named graph value and queues computed_output_changed on attached CC computers when the value changes. It runs on the computer thread, performs an integration side effect, does not yield, and is unavailable in preview. Unsupported or cyclic values and invalid channel names are errors. Example: ctx:endpoint("computercraft:channel"):call("publish", "status", { ready = true }).

docs.title: computercraft:peripheral/methods
docs.text: Signature: () -> table. The endpoint target is a computer-relative side. It returns the adjacent peripheral's sorted public method names, runs on the server tick thread, does not yield or mutate, and is unavailable in preview. Missing CC, invalid sides, and detached peripherals are errors. Call it through the bound shorthand: ctx:endpoint("computercraft:peripheral", "left"):methods().

docs.title: computercraft:peripheral/call
docs.text: Signature: (methodName: string, ...) -> table. It invokes a public CC API method and returns all results as an integer-keyed table. It runs on the server tick thread, may perform peripheral side effects, and may yield for main-thread tasks, MethodResult continuations, or queued events. It is unavailable in preview. Missing methods, unsupported values, detach, unload, and failed continuations are errors; prior outputs remain committed while suspended. Example: local result = ctx:endpoint("computercraft:peripheral", "left"):call("getEnergy").

docs.title: aeronautics:telemetry/measure
docs.text: Signature: () -> table. It returns telemetry for the nearest Create contraption (including Create Aeronautics structures) around the computer. The table has present (boolean), name and source (strings), x/y/z (contraption position), vx/vy/vz (contraption velocity), speed, distance, heading, pitch, roll, the heading frame hx/hy/hz, the right frame rx/ry/rz, and the angular velocity wx/wy/wz. It runs on the server tick thread, does not yield or mutate the world, and returns present = false with zeroed fields in preview. Missing Create Aeronautics is an error; when no contraption is within range present is false. Example: local telemetry = ctx:endpoint("aeronautics:telemetry"):call("measure").

docs.title: Computer Filesystem (computed:fs)
docs.text: Every computer owns an isolated CraftOS-style filesystem. Files live under the world save at <world>/computed/computer/<id>/, where <id> is the computer's numeric id (ComputerCraft-compatible: ids are allocated from <world>/computed/ids.json, which stores the last assigned id; the first computer gets 0). Computers with different ids never read each other's files and the tree travels with the world. There is no io/os global — everything goes through the computed:fs endpoint.

docs.title: Which folder belongs to which computer?
docs.text:
• On the item: the computer item shows Computer ID: <id> under its name, so dropped or stored computers keep their folder.
  • In the editor: the bottom-left corner shows Computer ID: <id> for the open computer.
  • From Lua: ctx:endpoint("computed:fs"):call("get_id") returns the numeric id (a number).
  • On disk: each root contains a computer.txt with the id, UUID, dimension, and block position.
  • Changing it: Import / Export → Set Computer ID in the editor assigns a chosen id (usable in survival). The filesystem switches to the new folder on the next tick (open handles are closed), and the id counter in ids.json moves forward so future computers never receive that id again. Computers that share an id also share their package folders (computed/packages/<id>).

docs.title: Quota
docs.text: Each computer filesystem is capped at 1 MiB. get_free_space reports the remaining bytes. Writes that would exceed the quota fail with an error; delete or overwrite to free space.

docs.title: Paths
docs.text: Paths are absolute-ish strings under the computer root. / and empty paths mean the root. . segments are skipped and .. clamps at the root (it cannot escape the computer). Segments are sanitized; control characters and Windows-illegal characters become _.

docs.title: Top-level methods
docs.text:
local fs = ctx:endpoint("computed:fs")

local id    = fs:call("get_id")             -- this computer's numeric id (number)
local names = fs:call("list", "/")          -- array of entry names
local ok    = fs:call("exists", "/data.txt")
local isDir = fs:call("is_dir", "/logs")
local size  = fs:call("get_size", "/data.txt")
local free  = fs:call("get_free_space", "/")
fs:call("make_dir", "/logs")
fs:call("move", "/old.txt", "/new.txt")
fs:call("copy", "/data.txt", "/backup.txt")
fs:call("delete", "/tmp.txt")
local path  = fs:call("combine", "/", "logs", "run.txt")
local parent = fs:call("get_dir", "/logs/run.txt")
local name  = fs:call("get_name", "/logs/run.txt")

docs.title: File handles
docs.text:
open(path, mode) returns a handle table. Modes: r, w, a (text) and rb, wb, ab (binary). Handles work with . or : calls.

local handle = fs:call("open", "/note.txt", "w")
handle:write_line("hello")
handle:flush()
handle:close()

local reader = fs:call("open", "/note.txt", "r")
local line = reader:read_line()   -- nil at EOF
local rest = reader:read_all()    -- nil at EOF
reader:close()

local binary = fs:call("open", "/blob.bin", "rb")
local chunk = binary:read_bytes(16)  -- raw bytes as a string; nil at EOF
binary:seek("set", 0)
binary:close()

Handle methods: read_line(), read_all(), read(count), read_bytes(count), write(text), write_line(text), seek(whence, offset) with set/cur/end, flush(), close(). Reads return nil at EOF. Writing on a read handle or reading on a write handle is an error. Closing twice is safe.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text: Open handles are flushed and closed when the computer unloads (block removed, program replaced, world unload). The filesystem itself is never deleted automatically.

docs.title: Graph events
docs.text:
Event Sender and Event Receiver provide named, wireless communication inside one computer graph. Every receiver whose Event name exactly matches a sender receives that sender's event.

Event Sender has a Boolean trigger and emits on its rising edge. Event Receiver exposes an Event output named triggered. Connect that output to the Event input on side-effect nodes such as Redstone Output or Run Command.

Both event nodes have configurable payload pins:

  • + adds a payload pin, up to 16.
  • - removes the last payload pin without renumbering the remaining stable IDs.
  • The payload control cycles the newest pin through number, boolean, string, table, and widget.

Sender and Receiver payload pins correspond by their stable data_N names. A receiver may declare only the fields it needs; additional sender fields are ignored. Use the same type for a given field on both sides.

Monitor uses the same + and - controls for one to 16 widget inputs. The Terminal widget accepts one configurable line input per pin (line_N), and the Table widget one configurable row input per pin (row_N).

Delivery order is deterministic. The scheduler indexes named receivers, so unrelated graph sections are not scanned for each event. Events emitted by an event handler are deferred to the next graph tick, and the pending queue is bounded to prevent an event feedback loop from hanging the server.

docs.title: Import and Export
docs.text:
The graph toolbar has one Import / Export menu beside the zoom controls. It keeps graph and node package actions together (plus Set Computer ID, which lets computers share those folders) and uses the same hover and selection treatment as the editor's other menus. Graph and node packages live in the world save under <world>/computed/packages/<id>/graphs/ and <world>/computed/packages/<id>/nodes/, scoped to the computer's ID: computers that share an ID share the same folders, while other IDs cannot see them; all transfers go through the server, which also works on dedicated servers. Import presents the available .computed files and export asks for a name. Existing files can be overwritten or saved with the next (n) suffix. Packages are limited to 1 MB per file. A graph package is a validated ZIP archive containing manifest.json, graph.json, and only the embedded Lua definitions used by the graph. Older exports that still sit in the game directory's computed/ folder are copied into the computer's package folders automatically the first time a package dialog is used (once per computer ID; existing world files are never overwritten).

Both graphs/ and nodes/ inside a computer's package folder support subfolders. The import dialog shows folders first and lets you browse into them (.. returns to the parent). Export names may include a path such as planes/racers/sprint; intermediate folders are created automatically. Existing user folders in the world save are picked up without conversion.

Programs can also travel on a Program Disk (an iron ingot, paper, and redstone make four disks):

The export dialog offers a Disk button beside Save, and Export Selected Node becomes Export Node to Disk while a disk is available. A disk can be held in the main hand or inserted into the computer's drive slot — shift-right-click the computer to open the peripheral bay, where the rightmost slot is the drive (shift-right-click while holding a disk inserts it directly). Exporting prefers the hand disk and falls back to the drive. The disk stores one package — a full graph archive or a single node source — as item data, and writing to it always replaces its previous content (the result reads Saved to disk as …). In the import dialogs a matching disk appears as the first entry whether it is held or inserted, so another player can load the program directly, even with a different computer ID.

Blank disks stack up to 16. A written disk glows and always stacks alone, and writing to a held stack writes exactly one disk while the rest stay blank. To wipe a written disk, craft it by itself in any crafting grid — the result is a blank disk again.

Right-click a written disk in your hand to toggle autostart: the action bar confirms Disk autostart: on, the tooltip gains an aqua Autostart: on line, and inserting the disk announces Disk inserted — autostart armed. The flagged disk loads and runs its graph as soon as it sits in the drive of a computer with an empty program — at insertion time or at the first tick after startup. A program already loaded on the computer always wins; eject it first to let the disk start.

Node source files use the computer's nodes/ folder and the .lua extension. Import Node is in the toolbar menu, while Export Selected Node is available there and in a user node's right-click menu. Import opens the selected Lua file in the Lua editor; export writes the source directly using the selected user node's title. Bundled and integration nodes cannot be exported, edited, or deleted.

Selected canvas nodes support Ctrl+C, Ctrl+X, and Ctrl+V. Pasted nodes are placed at the cursor and retain connections between nodes in the copied selection. Ctrl+D immediately clones the selection 24 pixels right and down; repeated presses continue from the latest clone to form a ladder.

The Lua editor also supports normal text selection and clipboard shortcuts. Use Ctrl+C to copy selected source and Ctrl+V to paste into editable user definitions. Paste Lua remains available from the empty-canvas context menu for clipboard imports.

For a new in-game definition, choose User Nodes → New Lua Node… in the Node Explorer. Saving the starter stores the source in the current computer and places the first instance.

Server validation checks the 64 KiB source limit, API version, definition ID, schema, hash, permissions, and the 256 embedded-definition limit. An identical ID/hash is a no-op. The same ID with different source requires explicit confirmation.

After replacement, instances recompile. Connections survive only when direction, stable port ID, and connection type all match. Removed or changed ports are reported before save.

CMP1, CMP2, format-2 graphs, JSON custom nodes, Functions, and Sections are not importable. Loading legacy world data initializes an empty format-3 program without backup.

docs.title: Live Preview
docs.text:
The focused Lua editor compiles 250 milliseconds after the last edit. Validation runs in order: syntax, definition contract, schema, then endpoint availability.

The right pane uses the production semantic palette, padded content layout, and control-aware node sizing. Sample inputs and fields are editable. Running the preview advances isolated preview ticks and state; Reset recreates the node from its defaults.

When source becomes invalid, the last valid preview remains visible, dimmed, and marked stale. Inline diagnostics describe the new invalid source. Preview endpoint calls use deterministic fixtures. Methods without fixtures, including command side effects, return an unavailable error and never touch a world.

Saving source is separate from preview: the server recompiles it, checks permissions and size, and only then replaces the embedded definition.

docs.title: Lua API Reference
docs.text: All methods execute on the computer thread. Definition methods have no side effects, are available during preview validation, return the same node for chaining, and fail when called after validation.

docs.title: computed.node(apiVersion, id, title)
docs.text: Parameters: integer API version (1), namespaced definition ID, and display title. Returns a mutable definition builder. Errors on unsupported versions, invalid IDs, invalid titles, or a second node in the same file. Preview behavior is identical to production. Example: local node = computed.node(1, "example:add", "Add").

docs.title: node:category(name)
docs.text: Sets the stable semantic category or nested category path. The default is utility. Errors on blank or overlong names. It selects a named renderer palette and has no runtime side effect. Example: node:category("math/arithmetic").

docs.title: node:style(style)
docs.text: Sets standard, compact, source, or sink; the default is standard. Errors on unknown styles. Example: node:style("compact").

docs.title: node:input(id, type, options)
docs.text: Adds an input. options is optional; required defaults to true and default defaults to nil. Type is number, boolean, string, event, widget, or table. Errors on duplicate IDs or invalid values. Example: node:input("value", "number", { default = 0 }).

docs.title: node:output(id, type, options)
docs.text: Adds an output with the same option and type rules as inputs. Outputs retain their last committed value after errors or yields. Example: node:output("result", "number").

docs.title: node:field(id, fieldType, options)
docs.text: Adds a number, text, boolean, choice, color, direction, or item field. Every field is rendered as an editable control inside each node instance. Options include default, an optional display label, numeric min/max, a positive numeric step, and choices for choice fields. visible_when = { field = "mode", equals = "advanced" } conditionally shows a field while preserving its value when hidden. Number fields default to control = "value"; control = "slider" requires finite min and max values with max > min. Text uses a value box, booleans use toggles, choice and direction fields use dropdowns, colors use ARGB hexadecimal controls, and items open the searchable item picker. Errors on invalid defaults, ranges, steps, controls, visibility references, or empty choice lists. Example: node:field("gain", "number", { default = 1, min = 0, max = 4, control = "slider", step = 0.1, label = "Gain" }).

docs.title: node:state(id, defaultValue)
docs.text: Declares persistent state with a serializable default. Returns the node. Errors on duplicate IDs or unsupported values during validation/persistence. Example: node:state("count", 0).

docs.title: node:execution(policy)
docs.text: Sets input, tick, step, or event; the default is input. Returns the node and errors on an unknown policy. Example: node:execution("tick").

docs.title: node:on_run(callback)
docs.text: Installs the single run callback. Returns the node. Errors when declared twice or when the value is not a function. The callback runs transactionally. Example: node:on_run(function(ctx) ctx:output("ok", true) end).

docs.title: node:on_event(eventName, callback)
docs.text:
Installs one named event callback. Returns the node. Errors on an invalid or duplicate event name. The callback receives ctx followed by emitted arguments. Example: node:on_event("reset", function(ctx) ctx:set_state("count", 0) end).

Context methods are available only inside callbacks. Reads have no side effects; writes stage changes until successful return.

docs.title: ctx:input(id)
docs.text: Returns the current connected or default input. Errors on malformed calls. Preview returns the editable sample input. Example: local speed = ctx:input("speed").

docs.title: ctx:inputs()
docs.text: Returns a copy of all current inputs keyed by stable port ID, including configurable per-node ports. Example: for id, value in pairs(ctx:inputs()) do ... end.

docs.title: ctx:output(id, value)
docs.text: Stages an output and returns nothing. Errors if the value cannot later be serialized. Preview updates the real renderer sample. Example: ctx:output("result", 4).

docs.title: ctx:field(id)
docs.text: Returns the authoritative field or its default. Preview returns the editable sample field. Example: local color = ctx:field("color").

docs.title: ctx:state(id)
docs.text: Returns an isolated copy of committed state. Mutating a returned table does not commit it; use set_state. Example: local count = ctx:state("count").

docs.title: ctx:set_state(id, value)
docs.text: Stages persistent state and returns nothing. Errors on unknown or non-serializable state. It commits only after callback success. Example: ctx:set_state("count", count + 1).

docs.title: ctx:endpoint(id, target)
docs.text: Returns a safe endpoint proxy. target is optional and defaults to an empty target. Errors on unknown endpoints. Preview uses fixtures or reports unavailable; it never performs production side effects. Example: local world = ctx:endpoint("computed:world").

docs.title: ctx:emit(eventName, ...)
docs.text: Queues a named graph event with serializable arguments and returns nothing. Delivery is deterministic after the current graph pass. Preview delivers inside the isolated preview graph. Example: ctx:emit("changed", 12).

docs.title: ctx:tick()
docs.text: Returns the current non-negative computer tick as an integer. It has no side effects and preview uses the preview tick. Example: local now = ctx:tick().

docs.title: ctx:graph_step()
docs.text: Returns the current deterministic graph step as an integer. It has no side effects. Example: local order = ctx:graph_step().

docs.title: ctx:is_preview()
docs.text: Returns true only in the isolated live preview. It has no side effects. Production logic should prefer endpoint policies over branching on this value. Example: if ctx:is_preview() then ... end.

docs.title: endpoint:methods()
docs.text: Returns an alphabetically stable array of method IDs. Bound dynamic endpoints such as computercraft:peripheral instead return methods exposed by the selected target. It has no side effects. Static endpoint metadata is available in preview; dynamic target discovery may be unavailable. Example: for _, name in ipairs(endpoint:methods()) do ... end.

docs.title: endpoint:call(methodName, ...)
docs.text: Validates arguments and invokes the registered handler. It returns the declared values, may yield only when the policy permits, and errors on unavailable previews, signature mismatches, handler failures, or invalid return values. Side effects and execution side are method-specific. Example: local time = world:call("time").

docs.title: Sandbox and Execution Budgets
docs.text:
Each computer owns one Lua VM. Every node instance receives an isolated environment and state map. Compiled prototypes are globally cached by API version and SHA-256 source hash.

Available libraries are base primitives, math, string, table, bit32, and coroutine. The runtime does not expose io, os, debug, package, require, load, loadfile, dofile, or luajava. Java reflection and arbitrary Java objects are unreachable.

File access is available only through the computed:fs endpoint. Every computer owns an isolated directory tree under the world save (<world>/computed/computer/<id>/); one computer can never see another computer's files. Each computer filesystem has a 1 MiB quota (get_free_space reports the remainder). Previews never touch the filesystem.

Each node invocation is limited to 50,000 Lua instructions. Each computer is limited to 500,000 Lua instructions per game tick. The private hook cannot be read or replaced by Lua. Limit errors abort the offending invocation, retain committed values, add an inline runtime diagnostic, and permit a later policy-driven retry.

Unloading a computer or replacing/removing a definition cancels its yielded coroutines.

docs.title: Types and State Serialization
docs.text:
Connection types are number, boolean, string, event, widget, and table. Connections require exactly matching types and each input accepts at most one edge.

Persistent values support Lua nil, booleans, finite numbers, strings, and acyclic tables. Table keys must be strings or integers. The maximum table depth is 16 and all program data shares the four-megabyte limit.

Functions, userdata, threads, cyclic tables, non-finite numbers, fractional numeric keys, and unsupported Java values are rejected. A serialization failure fails only the invocation and preserves the last committed state and outputs.

State is copied into an invocation. ctx:set_state stages a replacement; successful callback return commits the entire staged map. Yielded callbacks keep staged changes private until resumption completes.
